research_study_list.full_text: Low-Precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics Ruqi Zhang1 Andrew Gordon Wilson2 Christopher De Sa3 Abstract While low-precision optimization has been widely used to accelerate deep learning, low-precision sampling remains largely unexplored. As a con- sequence, sampling is simply infeasible in many large-scale scenarios, despite providing remark- able beneﬁts to generalization and uncertainty es- timation for neural networks. In this paper, we provide the ﬁrst study of low-precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD), showing that its costs can be signiﬁcantly reduced with- out sacriﬁcing performance, due to its intrinsic ability to handle system noise. We prove that the convergence of low-precision SGLD with full- precision gradient accumulators is less affected by the quantization error than its SGD counter- part in the strongly convex setting. To further en- able low-precision gradient accumulators, we de- velop a new quantization function for SGLD that preserves the variance in each update step. We demonstrate that low-precision SGLD achieves comparable performance to full-precision SGLD with only 8 bits on a variety of deep learning tasks. 1. Introduction Low-precision optimization has become increasingly popu- lar in reducing computation and memory costs of training deep neural networks (DNNs). It uses fewer bits to represent numbers in model parameters, activations, and gradients, and thus can drastically lower resource demands (Gupta et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2016; De Sa et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017). Prior work has shown that using 8-bit numbers in training DNNs achieves about 4 ×latency speed ups and memory reduction compared to 32-bit numbers on a wide variety of deep learning tasks (Sun et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018b; Banner et al., 2018). As datasets and architectures grow rapidly, performing low-precision 1The University of Texas at Austin 2New York Univer- sity 3Cornell University. Correspondence to: Ruqi Zhang <ruqiz@utexas.edu>. Proceedings of the 39 th International Conference on Machine Learning, Baltimore, Maryland, USA, PMLR 162, 2022. Copy- right 2022 by the author(s). optimization enables training large-scale DNNs efﬁciently and enables many applications on different hardware and platforms. Despite the impressive progress in low-precision optimiza- tion, low-precision sampling remains largely unexplored. However, we believe stochastic gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo (SGMCMC) methods (Welling & Teh, 2011; Chen et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2015) are particularly suited for low-precision arithmetic because of their intrinsic ro- bustness to system noise. In particular: (1) SGMCMC ex- plores weight space instead of converging to a single point, thus it should not require precise weights or gradients; (2) SGMCMC even adds noise to the system to encourage ex- ploration and so is naturally more tolerant to quantization noise; (3) SGMCMC performs Bayesian model averaging during testing using an ensemble of models, which allows coarse representations of individual models to be compen- sated by the overall model average (Zhu et al., 2019). SGMCMC is particularly compelling in Bayesian deep learning due to its ability to characterize complex and multi- modal DNN posteriors, providing state-of-the-art general- ization accuracy and calibration (Zhang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2016; Gan et al., 2017; Heek & Kalchbrenner, 2019). More- over, low-precision approaches are especially appealing in this setting, where at test time we must store samples from a posterior over millions of parameters, and perform multiple forward passes through the corresponding models, which incurs signiﬁcant memory and computational expenses. In this paper, we give the ﬁrst comprehensive study of low-precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) (Welling & Teh, 2011), providing both theoreti- cal convergence bounds and promising empirical results in deep learning. On strongly log-concave distributions (i.e. strongly convex functions for SGD), we prove that the convergence of SGLD with full-precision gradient ac- cumulators is more robust to the quantization error than its counterpart in SGD. Surprisingly, we ﬁnd that SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators can diverge arbitrarily far away from the target distribution with small stepsizes. We identify the source of the issue and develop a new quan- tization function to correct the bias with minimal overhead. Empirically, we demonstrate low-precision SGLD across different tasks, showing that it is able to provide superior arXiv:2206.09909v1  [cs.LG]  20 Jun 2022Low-Precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics generalization and uncertainty estimation using just 8 bits. We summarize our contributions as follows: • We provide a methodology for SGLD to leverage low- precision computation, including a new quantization function, while still guaranteeing its convergence to the target distribution. • We offer theoretical results which explicitly show how quantization error affects the convergence of the sam- pler in the strongly convex setting, proving its robust- ness to quantization noise over SGD. • We show SGLD is particularly suitable for low- precision deep learning over a range of experiments, including logistic regression, Bayesian neural networks on image and text classiﬁcation. In short, low-precision SGLD is often a compelling alter- native to standard SGLD, improving speed and memory efﬁciency, while retaining accuracy. Moreover, SGLD is ar- guably more amenable to low-precision computations than SGD. Our code is available here. 2. Related Work To speed up SGLD training, most existing work is on dis- tributed learning with synchronous or asynchronous commu- nication (Ahn et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019). Another direction is to shorten training time by accelerating the convergence using variance reduction techniques (Dubey et al., 2016; Baker et al., 2019), importance sampling (Deng et al., 2020) or a cyclical learning rate schedule (Zhang et al., 2020). To speed up SGLD during testing, distillation techniques are often used to save both compute and memory which transfer the knowledge of an ensemble of models to a single model (Korattikara et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018a). Low-precision computation has become one of the most common approaches to reduce latency and memory con- sumption in deep learning and is widely supported on new emerging chips including CPUs, GPUs and TPUs (Micike- vicius et al., 2018; Krishnamoorthi, 2018; Esser et al., 2020). Two main directions to improve low-precision training in- clude developing new number formats (Sun et al., 2019; 2020) or studying mixed-precision schemes (Courbariaux et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2016; Banner et al., 2018). Re- cently, one line of work applies the Bayesian framework to learn a deterministic quantized neural network (Soudry et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2015; Achterhold et al., 2018; van Baalen et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2020). Low-precision computation is largely unexplored for Bayesian neural networks, despite their speciﬁc promise in this domain. Su et al. (2019) proposes a method to train binarized variational BNNs, and Cai et al. (2018) devel- ops efﬁcient hardware for training low-precision variational BNNs. The only work on low-precision MCMC known to us is Ferianc et al. (2021), which directly applies post- training quantization techniques from optimization (Jacob et al., 2018) to convert BNNs trained by Stochastic Gradi- ent Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Chen et al., 2014) into low- precision models. We instead study training low-precision models by SGLD from scratch, to accelerate both training and testing. 3. Preliminaries 3.1. Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics In the Bayesian setting, given some dataset D, a model with parameters θ ∈Rd, and a prior p(θ), we are interested in sampling from the posterior p(θ|D) ∝exp(−U(θ)), where the energy function is U(θ) = − ∑ x∈D log p(x|θ) −log p(θ). When the dataset is large, the cost of computing a sum over the entire dataset is expensive. Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) (Welling & Teh, 2011) reduces the cost by using a stochastic gradient estimation ∇˜U, which is an unbiased estimator of∇Ubased on a subset of the datasetD. Speciﬁcally, SGLD updates the parameterθin the (k+1)-th step following the rule θk+1 = θk −α∇˜U(θk) + √ 2αξk+1, (1) where αis the stepsize and ξis a standard Gaussian noise. Compared to the SGD update, the only difference is that SGLD adds an additional Gaussian noise in each step, which essentially enables SGLD to characterize the full distribu- tion instead of converging to a single point. The close connection between SGLD and SGD makes it convenient to implement and run on existing deep learning tasks for which SGD is the typical learning algorithm. 3.2. Low-Precision Training We study training a low-precision model by SGLD from scratch, to reduce both training and testing costs. Speciﬁ- cally, we follow the framework in prior work to quantize the weights, activations, backpropagation errors, and gra- dients (Wu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018b; Yang et al., 2019). We mainly consider the effect of weight and gradient quantization following previous work (Li et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). Please refer to Appendix A for more details. 3.2.1. N UMBER REPRESENTATIONS To represent numbers in low-precision, one simple way is to use ﬁxed point, which has been utilized in both theory andLow-Precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics practice (Gupta et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). Speciﬁcally, suppose that we use W bits to represent numbers with F of those W bits to represent the fractional part. Then there is a distance between con- secutive representable numbers, ∆ = 2−F, which is called quantization gap. The representable numbers also have a lower bound land an upper bound u, where l= −2W−F−1, u = 2W−F−1 −2−F. As shown above, when the number of bits decreases, the accuracy of number representation decreases. We use this type of number representation in our theoretical analysis and empirical demonstration following previous work (Li et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). Another common type of number representation is ﬂoating point where each number has its own exponent part. Be- tween ﬁxed point and ﬂoating point, there is block ﬂoating point which allows all numbers within a block to share the same exponent (Song et al., 2018). We use block ﬂoating point for deep learning experiments since it has been shown more favorable for deep models (Yang et al., 2019). 3.2.2. Q UANTIZATION Having low-precision number representation in hand, we also need a quantization function Qto convert a real-valued number into a low-precision number. Such functions include deterministic roundingand stochastic rounding. Particularly, the deterministic rounding function Qd quantizes a number to its nearest representable neighbor as follows: Qd(θ) = sign(θ) ·clip ( ∆ ⌊|θ| ∆ + 1 2 ⌋ ,l,u ) , where clip(x,l,u ) = max(min(x,u),l). Instead, stochas- tic rounding Qsquantizes a number with a probability based on the distance to its representable neighbor: Qs(θ) = { clip ( ∆ ⌊θ ∆ ⌋ ,l,u ) , w.p. ⌈θ ∆ ⌉ −θ ∆ clip ( ∆ ⌈θ ∆ ⌉ ,l,u ) , w.p. 1 − (⌈θ ∆ ⌉ −θ ∆ ) . An important property of Qs is that E[Qs(θ)] = θ, which means the quantized number is unbiased. Qs is generally preferred over Qd in practice since it can preserve gradient information especially when the gradient update is smaller than the quantization gap (Gupta et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018b). In what follows, we use QW and ∆W to denote the weights’ quantizer and quantization gap,QG and ∆G to denote gradients’ quantizer and quantization gap. To do the gradient update in low-precision training, there are two common choices depending on whether we store an additional copy of full-precision weights. Full-precision gradient accumulators use a full-precision weight buffer to accumulate gradient updates and only quantize weights before computing gradients. SGD with full-precision gra- dient accumulators (SGDLP-F) updates the weights as the following, θk+1 = θk −αQG ( ∇˜U(QW (θk)) ) , where we use full-precision θk+1 and θk in the update, and only quantize the weight for forward and backward propa- gation (Courbariaux et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017). However, gradient accumulators have to be frequently up- dated during training, therefore it will be ideal to also rep- resent it in low-precision to further reduce the costs. To achieve it, we could instead do the update as follows, θk+1 = QW ( θk −αQG ( ∇˜U(θk) )) , (2) where θis always represented in low-precision. This update of SGD is called using low-precision gradient accumulators (SGDLP-L). Both full- and low-precision gradient accu- mulators have been widely used: low-precision gradient accumulators are cheaper and faster because of having all numbers in low-precision, whereas full-precision gradient accumulators generally have better performance because of more precisely reﬂecting small gradient updates (Cour- bariaux et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017). 4. Low-Precision SGLD In this section, we ﬁrst study the convergence of low- precision SGLD with full-precision gradient accumulators (SGLDLP-F) on strongly log-concave distributions (i.e. the energy function is strongly convex) and show that SGLDLP- F is less affected by the quantization error than its SGD counterpart. Next we analyze low-precision SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators (SGLDLP-L) under the same setup and prove that SGLDLP-L can diverge ar- bitrarily far away from the target distribution with a small stepsize, which however is typically required by SGLD to reduce asymptotic bias. Finally, we solve this problem by developing a variance-corrected quantization function and further prove that with this quantization function, SGLDLP- L converges with small stepsizes. 4.1. Full-Precision Gradient Accumulators As shown in Equation (1), the update of SGLD is simply a SGD update plus a Gaussian noise. Therefore the low- precision formulation for SGD in Section 3.2 can be nat- urally extended to SGLD training. Similar to SGDLP-F, we can do low-precision SGLD with full-precision gradient accumulators (SGLDLP-F) as the following: θk+1 = θk −αQG ( ∇˜U(QW (θk)) ) + √ 2αξk+1, (3)Low-Precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics which can also be viewed as SGDLP-F plus a Gaussian noise in each step. However, the Gaussian noise turns out to help counter-effect the noise introduced by quantization, making SGLDLP-F more robust to inaccurate number repre- sentation and converging better than SGDLP-F as we show later in this section. We now prove the convergence of SGLDLP-F. Our analysis is built upon the 2-Wasserstein distance bounds of SGLD in Dalalyan & Karagulyan (2019), where the target distri- bution is assumed to be smooth and strongly log-concave. We additionally assume the energy function has Lipschitz Hessian following recent work in low-precision optimiza- tion (Yang et al., 2019). In summary, the energy function U has the following assumptions, ∀θ,θ′∈Rd, it satisﬁes    U(θ) −U(θ′) −∇U(θ′)⊺(θ−θ′) ≥(m/2) ∥θ−θ′∥2 2 , ∥∇U(θ) −∇U(θ′)∥2 ≤M∥θ−θ′∥2 , ∥∇2U(θ) −∇2U(θ′)∥2 ≤Ψ∥θ−θ′∥2, for some positive constants m, M and Ψ. We further as- sume that the variance of the stochastic gradient is bounded E[∥∇˜U(θ) −∇U(θ)∥2 2] ≤κ2 for some constant κ. For simplicity, we consider SGLD with a constant stepsize α. We use stochastic rounding for quantizing both weights and gradients as it is generally better than deterministic rounding and has also been used in previous low-precision theoretical analysis (Li et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). Theorem 1. We run SGLDLP-F under the above assump- tions and with a constant stepsize α ≤2/(m+ M). Let π be the target distribution, µ0 be the initial distribution and µK be the distribution obtained by SGLDLP-F after K iterations, then the 2-Wasserstein distance is W2(µK,π) ≤(1 −αm)KW2(µ0,π) + 1.65(M/m)(αd)1/2 + min ( Ψ∆2 Wd 4m ,M∆W √ d 2m ) + √ (∆2 G+ M2∆2 W)αd+ 4ακ2 4m . This theorem shows that SGLDLP-F converges to the accu- racy ﬂoor min ( Ψ∆2 W d 4m ,M∆W √ d 2m ) given large enough num- ber of iterations Kand small enough stepsize α. Besides, if we further assume that the energy function is quadratic, that is Ψ = 0, then SGLDLP-F converges to the target distribu- tion asymptotically. This matches the result of SGDLP-F on a quadratic function which converges to the optimum asymptotically (Li et al., 2017). Our theorem also recovers the bound in Dalalyan & Karagulyan (2019) when the quan- tization gap is zero (we ignore 1.65M in the denominator in their bound for simplicity). However, when the energy function is not quadratic, the convergence of SGLDLP-F to the target distribution has a O(∆2 W) rate whereas SGDLP-F to the optimum has a O(∆W) rate (Yang et al., 2019)1. Recall that ∆W = 2−F where F is the number of fractional bits, our result suggests that asymptotically, SGLD only needs half the number of bits as SGD needs to achieve the same convergence accu- racy! Our comparison between SGLD and SGD also ﬁts into the literature in comparing sampling and optimization convergence bounds (Ma et al., 2019; Talwar, 2019) (see Appendix E for more details). In summary, our theorem implies how sensitive SGLD is to the quantization error, and actually suggests that sampling methods are more suitable with low-precision computation than optimization methods. 4.2. Low-Precision Gradient Accumulators As mentioned before, it will be ideal to further reduce the costs using low-precision gradient accumulators. Mimick- ing the update of SGDLP-L in Equation (2), it is natural to get the following update rule for SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators (SGLDLP-L), θk+1 = QW ( θk −αQG ( ∇˜U(θk) ) + √ 2αξk+1 ) . (4) Surprisingly, while we can prove a convergence result for SGLDLP-L, our theory and empirical results suggest that it can diverge arbitrarily far away from the target distribution with small stepsizes. Theorem 2. We run SGLDLP-L under the same assump- tions as in Theorem 1. Let µ0 be the initial distribution and µK be the distribution obtained by SGLDLP-L after K iterations, then W2(µK,π) ≤(1 −αm)KW2(µ0,π) + 1.65(M/m)(αd)1/2 + min ( Ψ∆2 Wd 4m ,M∆W √ d 2m ) + A+ ( (1 −αm)K + 1 )∆W √ d 2 , where A= √ (α∆2 G+α−1∆2 W )d+4ακ2 4m . Since the term Acontains α−1 in the numerator, this theo- rem implies that as the stepsize αdecreases, W2 distance between the stationary distribution of SGLDLP-L and the target distribution may increase. To test if this is the case, we empirically run SGLDLP-L on a standard Gaussian dis- tribution in Figure 1. We use 8-bit ﬁxed point and assign 3 of them to represent the fractional part. Our results verify that SGLDLP-L indeed diverges from the target distribution with small stepsizes. In the same time, SGLDLP-F always converges to the target distribution with different stepsizes, aligning with the result in Theorem 1. Moreover, enabling a small stepsize in SGLD is often desirable, since it is needed to reduce the asymptotic bias of the posterior approximation (Welling & Teh, 2011). 4.3. Variance-Corrected Quantization To approach correcting the problem with the na¨ıve SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators, we ﬁrst need to identify the source of the issue. We show in the following that the reason is the variance of each dimension of θk+1 becomes larger due to using low-precision gradient accumu- lators. Speciﬁcally, given the stochastic gradient ∇˜U, the update of full-precision SGLD can be viewed as sampling from a Gaussian distribution for each dimension i θk+1,i ∼N ( θk,i −α∇˜U(θk)i,2α ) ,for i= 1,··· ,d. Since stochastic rounding is unbiased, using it as the weight quantizer QW and the gradient quantizer QG in SGLDLP-L gives us E[θk+1,i] = E [ QW ( θk,i −αQG ( ∇˜U(θk) ) i + √ 2αξk+1,i )] = θk,i −α∇˜U(θk)i, which has the same mean as θk+1 in full-precision. How- ever, the variance of θk+1,i is now essentially larger than needed. If we ignore the variance from QG and the stochas- tic gradient, since they are present and have been shown to work well in SGLDLP-F, the variance of θk+1,i is Var [θk+1,i] = E [ Var [ QW ( θk,i −α∇U(θk)i + √ 2αξk+1,i )⏐⏐⏐ξk+1,i ]] + Var [ E [ QW ( θk,i −α∇U(θk)i + √ 2αξk+1,i )⏐⏐⏐ξk+1,i ]] = ∆2 W 4 χk+1,i + 2α. where χk+1,i ∈[0,1] depends on the distance of θk+1,i to its discrete neighbor. The above equation shows that the variance in SGLDLP-L update is larger than the right vari- ance value 2α. Empirically, from Figure 1, we can also ﬁnd that na ¨ıve SGLDLP-L estimates the mean correctly but variance wrongly. This validates our intuition that low- precision gradient accumulators with stochastic rounding adds more variance than needed leading to an inaccurate variance estimation. Besides, we cannot simply use deter- ministic rounding to solve the problem, since it is a biased estimation and generally provides much worse results than stochastic rounding especially on deep neural networks (see Appendix F for an empirical demonstration). To enable SGLD with low-precision gradient accumula- tors, we propose a new quantization function Qvc, denoting variance-corrected quantization, to ﬁx the issue. The main idea of Qvc is to directly sample from the discrete weight space instead of quantizing a real-valued Gaussian sample. First we note that if we want a sample with mean µ≥0 and variance v≤∆2 W/4, we could sample from the followingLow-Precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics Algorithm 1Variance-Corrected Low-Precision SGLD (VC SGLDLP-L). given: Stepsize α, number of training iterations K, gra- dient quantizer QG and quantization gap of weights ∆W. for k= 1 : Kdo update θk+1 ←Qvc ( θk −αQG ( ∇˜U(θk) ) ,2α,∆W ) end for output: samples {θk} categorical distribution over {∆W,−∆W,0}to get it, Cat(µ,v) =    ∆W, w.p. v+µ2+µ∆W 2∆2 W −∆W, w.p. v+µ2−µ∆W 2∆2 W 0, otherwise (5) Now we show how to use this categorical distribution to pre- serve the correct mean and variance for quantized θk+1. We do so considering two cases: when the Gaussian variance 2αis larger than the largest possible stochastic rounding variance ∆2 W/4, Qvc ﬁrst adds a small Gaussian noise and uses a sample from Equation (5) to make up the remain- ing variance; in the other situation, Qvc directly samples from Equation (5) to achieve the target variance. The full description of Qvc is outlined in Algorithm 2. Our variance-corrected quantization function Qvc always guarantees the correct mean,E[θk+1,i] = θk,i−α∇˜U(θk)i, and further guarantees the correct variance Var [θk+1,i] = 2αmost of the time except when v = 2α < vs. However that case rarely happens in practice, because the stepsize has to be extremely small. Besides, our quantization is simple to implement and its cost is negligible compared to gradient computation. Although Qvc only preserves the correctness of the ﬁrst two moments (i.e. mean and variance), we show that this does not affect the performance much in both theory and practice. MNIST Logistic Regression We ﬁrst empirically verify our the- orems, including the bias dependence on the quantization levels and the tightness of the bounds, on a logistic regres- sion on MNIST dataset. We use N(0,1/6) as the prior distribution following Yang et al. (2019) and the resulting posterior distribution is strongly log-concave and satisﬁes the assumptions in Section 4. We use ﬁxed point numbers with 2 integer bits and vary the number of fractional bits which is corresponding to varying the quantization gap ∆. We report test negative log-likelihood (NLL) with different numbers of fractional bits in Figure 2a. From the results, we see that SGLDLP-F is more robust to the decay of the number of bits than its SGD counter- part since SGLDLP-F outperforms SGDLP-F on all number of bits and recovers the full-precision result with 6 bits whereas SGDLP-F needs 10 bits. This veriﬁes Theorem 1 that SGLDLP-F converges to the target distribution up to an error and is more robust to the quantization gap than SGDLP-F. This also shows that the bound in Theorem 1 is relatively tight in terms of the quantization gap since SGLDLP-F needs roughly half number of bits compared to SGDLP-F to achieve the same convergence accuracy. With low-precision gradient accumulators, we can see that VC SGLDLP-L is signiﬁcantly better than na¨ıve SGLDLP-L, in- dicating that our variance-corrected quantization effectively reduces the bias of gradient accumulators, which veriﬁes Theorem 2 and Theorem 3. Moreover, VC SGLDLP-L outperforms SGDLP-L on all numbers of bits and even out- performs SGDLP-F when using 2 fractional bits. These ob- servations demonstrate that with either full- or low-precision gradient accumulators, SGLD is able to maintain its high performance whereas SGD deteriorates quickly as the quan- tization noise increases. Multilayer Perceptron To test whether these results ap- ply to non-log-concave distributions, we replace the logis- tic regression model by a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP). The MLP has 100 hidden units and RELU non- linearities. From Figure 2b, we observe similar results as on the logistic regression, suggesting that empirically our analysis still stands on general distributions and sheds light on the possibility of extending the theoretical analysis of low-precision SGLD to non-log-concave settings. Please note that as far as we understand, there is no theoretical con- vergence result of low-precision optimization in non-convex settings either. 5.2. Block Floating Point We also consider block ﬂoating point (BFP) which is another common number type and is often preferred over ﬁxed point on deep models due to less quantization error caused by overﬂow and underﬂow (Song et al., 2018). Following the block design in Yang et al. (2019), we use small-block for ResNet and big-block for LSTM. The Qvc function naturally generalizes to BFP and only needs a small modiﬁcation (see Appendix G for the algorithm of Qvc with BFP). By using BFP, the results of all low-precision methods improve over ﬁxed point. SGLDLP- F can match the performance of SGLDFP with all num- bers quantized to 8-bit except gradient accumulators. VC SGLDLP-L still outperforms na¨ıve SGLDLP-L indicating the effectiveness of Qvc with BFP. Again, SGLDFP-F and VC SGLDLP-L outperform their SGD counterparts on all tasks, suggesting the general applicability of low-precision SGLD with different number types. Cyclical SGLD We further apply low-precision to a re- cent variant of SGLD, cSGLD, which utilizes a cyclical learning rate schedule to speed up convergence (Zhang et al., 2020). We observe that the results of cSGLD-F are very close to those of cSGLDFP, and VC cSGLDLP-L can match or even outperforms full-precision SGD with all numbers quantized to 8 bits! These results indicate that diverse sam- ples from different modes, obtained by the cyclical learning rate schedule, can counter-effect the quantization error by providing complementary predictions. Expected Calibration Error Besides generalization per- formance, we further report the results of expected cali- bration error (ECE) (Guo et al., 2017) to demonstrate the uncertainty estimation of low-precision SGLD. In Table 2, we observe that SGLDLP-F and VC SGLDLP-L achieve al- most the same or even lower ECE than full-precision SGLD, showing the ability of SGLD to give well-calibrated predic- tions does not degenerate due to using low-precision. VC SGLDLP-L sometimes gives lower ECE than SGLDLP- F which may be due to the regularization effect of low- precision arithmetic. Moreover, cSGLD in low-precision not only achieves the best accuracy but also has the best calibration, further suggesting that diverse samples obtained by a cyclical learning rate schedule have a positive effect on quantization. SGLDLP-F vs VC SGLDLP-L We have provided two variants of low-precision SGLD for practical use. In general, SGLDLP-F has better performance while VC SGLDLP-L requires less computation, making them suitable for dif- ferent cases. When the computation resources are very limited, e.g. on edge devices, VC SGLDLP-L is preferred for saving computation while when the resources are able to support full-precision gradient accumulators, SGLDLP-F is preferred for better performance. 5.3. ImageNet Finally, we test low-precision SGLD on a large-scale im- age classiﬁcation dataset, ImageNet, with ResNet-18. We train SGD for 90 epochs and train SGLD for 10 epochs using the trained SGD model as the initialization. In Ta- ble 3, we observe that the improvement of SGLD over SGD is larger in low-precision (0.76% top-1 error) than in full- precision (0.17% top-1 error), showing the advantages of low-precision SGLD on large-scale deep learning tasks. We could not achieve reasonable results with low-precision gra- dient accumulators for SGD and SGLD, which might be caused by hyper-parameter tuning. 6. Conclusion We provide the ﬁrst comprehensive investigation for low- precision SGLD. With full-precision gradient accumulators, we prove that SGLD is convergent and can be safely used in practice, and further show that it has a better dependency of convergence on the quantization gap than SGD. More- over, we reveal issues in na¨ıvely performing low-precision computation in SGLD with low-precision gradient accumu- lators, and propose a new theoretically guaranteed quan- tization function to enable fully quantized sampling. We conduct experiments on a Gaussian distribution and a logis- tic regression to empirically verify our theoretical results. Besides, we show that low-precision SGLD achieves com- parable results with full-precision SGLD and outperforms low-precision SGD signiﬁcantly on several Bayesian deep learning benchmarks. MCMC was once the gold standard on small neural net- works (Neal et al., 2011), but has been signiﬁcantly limited by its high costs on large architectures in deep learning. We believe this work ﬁlls an important gap, and will accelerate the practical use of sampling methods on large-scale and resource-restricted machine learning problems. Moreover, low-precision SGLD could broadly be used as a drop-in replacement for standard SGLD, as it can confer speed and memory advantages, while retaining accuracy. Comparison to SGD Bounds There have been many works on comparing optimization and sampling algorithms since they serve as two main computational strategies for machine learning (Ma et al., 2019; Talwar, 2019). For example, in Ma et al. (2019), the authors compare the total variation distance between the approximate distribution and the target distribution (sampling bound), with the objective gap (optimization bound). Following previous work, we compare our 2-Wasserstein distance bound with previous SGD bounds. Previous low-precision SGD convergence bounds are shown in terms of the squared distance to the optimum¯θK −θ∗2 2 (Yang et al., 2019). In order to compare our bounds with theirs, we consider a 2-Wasserstein distance between two point distributions. Let µK be the point distribution assigns zero probability everywhere except ¯θK and πbe the point distribution assigns zero probability everywhere except θ∗. Therefore, our 2-Wasserstein distance is O(∆2 W) whereas SGD’s 2-Wasserstein distance isO(∆W), which shows SGLD is more robust to the quantization error. F. Deterministic Rounding vs Stochastic Rounding Compared to deterministic rounding, stochastic rounding is unbiased and thus can preserve gradient information even when the gradient update is smaller than the quantization gap. In theory, deterministic rounding will make the convergence bound worse due to its bias. For example, in Theorem 1, using deterministic rounding as the weight quantizer makes the bias term becomes O(∆w), which is worse than the current O(∆2 w). In practice, stochastic rounding generally provides much better results than deterministic rounding especially on deep neural networks (Gupta et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018b). For example, on CIFAR10 with 8-bit block ﬂoating point, we found that using deterministic rounding to quantize the weight in SGDLP-L and SGLDLP-L gives test errors 7.44% and 7.37% respectively, which are much worse than using stochastic rounding (SGDLP-L:5.86%, na¨ıve SGLDLP-L: 5.85%, VC SGLDLP-L: 5.51%). llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper provides the first comprehensive study of low-precision Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD), addressing the feasibility issues of sampling in large-scale scenarios. It proves that low-precision SGLD with full-precision gradient accumulators is more robust to quantization error than its SGD counterpart in the strongly convex setting, requiring roughly half the bits for comparable accuracy. The work identifies a critical divergence issue in naive low-precision SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators at small stepsizes and proposes a novel variance-corrected quantization function (Qvc) to resolve this, enabling fully quantized sampling with theoretical convergence guarantees. Empirically, the study demonstrates that low-precision SGLD achieves comparable generalization and uncertainty estimation performance to full-precision SGLD using only 8 bits across various deep learning tasks, significantly outperforming low-precision SGD.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The methodology involves analyzing two main variants of low-precision SGLD: SGLD with full-precision gradient accumulators (SGLDLP-F) and SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators (SGLDLP-L). Theoretical convergence bounds are derived using 2-Wasserstein distance, under assumptions of strongly log-concave (strongly convex) energy functions and Lipschitz Hessian, to demonstrate SGLD's robustness to quantization noise compared to SGD. To address the divergence of naive SGLDLP-L, a novel variance-corrected quantization function (Qvc) is introduced. Qvc ensures correct mean and variance in update steps by directly sampling from the discrete weight space, utilizing a categorical distribution to achieve the target variance. Both fixed-point and block floating-point number representations are employed for quantization, with a focus on 8-bit precision.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The research uses qtorch for simulating low-precision training across experiments. Quantization is applied to weights, gradients, activations, and backpropagation errors, primarily with 8-bit fixed-point and 8-bit block floating-point representations. Experiments include: 1) Logistic regression and a two-layer Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) on MNIST to verify theoretical convergence and bias dependence on quantization levels, reporting Test Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL). 2) ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and LSTM on IMDB for image and sentiment classification, evaluating Test Errors and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). 3) ResNet-18 on ImageNet, a large-scale image classification task, for Top-1 and Top-5 error rates. SGLD samples are collected from the posterior of model weights, and predictions are obtained via Bayesian model averaging. Comparisons are made against full-precision and low-precision SGD variants.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: A significant limitation identified is that naive low-precision SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators (SGLDLP-L) can diverge arbitrarily far from the target distribution, particularly with the small stepsizes typically required for SGLD to reduce asymptotic bias. While a variance-corrected quantization function (Qvc) is proposed to address this, its theoretical bound for convergence (O(√∆W)) is equivalent to that of low-precision SGD with low-precision gradient accumulators, with the paper noting room for improvement. Furthermore, low-precision activations were found to significantly harm performance in some 8-bit fixed-point experiments, necessitating the use of full-precision activations. On the large-scale ImageNet dataset, the study could not achieve reasonable results with low-precision gradient accumulators for either SGD or SGLD, suggesting potential challenges related to hyper-parameter tuning or inherent difficulties on such large tasks.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future research directions include improving the theoretical bound for the variance-corrected low-precision SGLD with low-precision gradient accumulators (VC SGLDLP-L). The empirical success of low-precision SGLD on non-log-concave distributions (like MLPs) suggests a promising avenue for extending the theoretical analysis of low-precision SGLD beyond strongly log-concave settings. Additionally, addressing the challenges associated with low-precision activations to achieve comparable performance without relying on full-precision activations could be an important direction. Overcoming difficulties in achieving reasonable results with low-precision gradient accumulators for SGD and SGLD on large-scale datasets like ImageNet, potentially through better hyper-parameter tuning or methodological refinements, is another area for future exploration.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Token–level mixed-precision for LLM inference is still an open problem.  Current 4-bit methods (e.g. NF4, GPTQ, AWQ) choose a single precision per weight‐group and often quantise activations to 8-bit uniformly.  This static choice wastes bandwidth on ‘easy’ tokens (e.g. punctuation, high-frequency function words) yet cannot protect the small set of ‘hard’ tokens that trigger chain-of-thought style reasoning or require long-range factual recall.  Attempts at dynamic schemes either work at layer level (DDQ) or rely on temporal information (TDQ) and do not address (1) per-token importance forecasting, (2) interaction with the KV-cache that lives throughout the whole context, and (3) hardware overhead when switching precision inside the kernel.  Solving this would simultaneously cut memory (smaller KV cache) and boost throughput while preserving accuracy on reasoning-heavy benchmarks.
Methods: We propose HAT-Q (Hierarchical Attention-aware Token Quantisation).  Key ideas:
1. Importance Predictor  –  a light, frozen linear probe that runs on the  hidden state h_t just produced by the model (no extra attention).  It outputs a 2-bit score s_t ∈ {0,1,2,3} denoting required precision budget for token t.
2. Hierarchical Precision Palette  –  weights are pre-quantised once into two palettes: P4 (NF4, 4-bit) and P8 (INT8).  Activations/KV elements are stored in 4-bit blocks by default; when s_t>1 the block is transiently up-cast to 8-bit by table look-up using the P8 palette already resident in L2.
3. Cache-Relayout  –  KV cache is written with the precision dictated by s_t but read with the max(s_{t_query}, s_{t_key}).  A cheap bit-packed header (2 bits per 16-token block) encodes the stored precision so that no branching is required in CUDA kernel.
4. Budgeted Error Fine-Tuning  –  post-training, we run a 512-sample calibration set and optimise the predictor thresholds with STE to satisfy a global accuracy loss budget (<0.3 on MMLU) while minimising expected 8-bit usage.
5. Kernel Support  –  extend bitsandbytes GEMM to accept a per-row 1-bit mask selecting 4-bit/8-bit tiles; tiles are processed in fixed order so warp divergence is avoided.
Novelty vs prior work: (a) first token-granular mixed precision for both activations and KV, (b) no run-time quant/dequant; only palette switch; (c) predictor is calibration-trained, so no re-training of the whole LLM; (d) compatible with existing NF4 weight loaders.
Experimental Setup: Models: Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B and Mistral-7B.
Datasets / Tasks:
• Knowledge & reasoning – MMLU (57 subs), HellaSwag, GSM8K (8-shot), ARC-c/e.
• Long-context – Longeval (16k), NarrativeQA-Long (32k subset).
Metrics:
• Accuracy / exact-match per task.
• Average precision budget = E[s_t] (lower is better).
• Throughput (tokens/s) and latency P50/P99 on A100-80G, CUDA 12.2.
• Peak and sustained GPU memory incl. KV cache.
Baselines: FP16, Static NF4 (bitsandbytes), SmoothQuant 8-bit, AWQ 4-bit, Bayesian Bits mixed-precision, and a naïve ‘critical-token 8-bit’ heuristic (entropy>threshold).
Ablations: (1) remove cache-relayout, (2) predictor replaced by random mask of same budget, (3) palette switch only on value-vectors.
Robustness: evaluate under prompt noise (token dropout 10 %), and adversarial punctuation injection.
Result: We expect HAT-Q to:
• Match or exceed static NF4 accuracy: <0.2 average drop on MMLU, <0.1 on HellaSwag; GSM8K exact-match within 0.3 %.  Significant gains over static 4-bit on long-context (+2-3 % EM on 32k NarrativeQA).
• Reduce average activation/KV precision to 4.6 bits (≈25 % of tokens stored in 8-bit) giving 28 % KV-cache memory saving vs uniform 8-bit and 12 % vs uniform 4-bit due to header compression.
• End-to-end throughput +18 % over static NF4 on 7B and +22 % on 13B; latency P99 improved by ~15 %.
• Ablations confirm importance predictor explains >80 % of accuracy retention; random mask fails.
• Robustness tests show <0.5 % additional degradation compared with FP16.
Conclusion: HAT-Q demonstrates that fine-grained, token-aware precision control is feasible without sacrificing hardware efficiency.  By marrying a learned importance predictor with a two-palette quantiser and cache-aware kernels, we simultaneously lower memory footprint and raise throughput while keeping reasoning accuracy intact.  The approach is orthogonal to weight-only compressors (GPTQ, AQLM) and can be combined with them for further gains.  Future work can explore (i) multi-palette extensions to include 2-bit proxies for very long contexts, (ii) training-time regularisers that directly optimise predictor scores, and (iii) ASIC designs where palette look-ups are fused into SRAM access, pushing token-adaptive inference towards real-time edge LLM deployment.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
1) Experiment A: End-to-end accuracy, throughput, and memory across diverse tasks
Goal / hypothesis
- Validate that HAT-Q preserves accuracy while improving throughput and memory use versus standard 4/8-bit baselines.
- Show that the importance predictor drives most of the accuracy retention at a lower average precision budget.

Models and HW
- Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, Mistral-7B (HF Transformers)
- A100-80G, CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.4+, bitsandbytes 0.43+, Triton 2.2+

Tasks and data
- Knowledge & reasoning: MMLU (57 subs), HellaSwag, GSM8K (8-shot), ARC-c/e via lm-eval-harness
- Optional sanity checks: Wikitext-2 perplexity

Baselines
- FP16 (transformers default)
- Static NF4 (bitsandbytes 4-bit) for weights + uniform 8-bit activations or uniform 4/8 KV cache
- SmoothQuant 8-bit (llm.int8), AWQ 4-bit
- Naive “critical-token 8-bit” using entropy threshold on logits
- If available: Bayesian Bits mixed-precision

HAT-Q implementation (Python-feasible)
- Weight palettes
  - Load model weights in FP16.
  - Pre-quantize per group into two palettes:
    - P4: NF4 quant via bitsandbytes (bnb.nn.Linear4bit) and expose the dequant LUT.
    - P8: INT8 per-channel symmetric quant; store per-channel scales and int8 weights in GPU memory. Use an 8-bit palette buffer (simulating residency in L2 by keeping it on device; reuse across layers).
- Importance predictor
  - A small linear probe: s_hat = W h_t + b, where W maps hidden_size -> 1. Convert to 2-bit score s_t in {0,1,2,3} by three thresholds tau.
  - Train W,b on a 5–10M token calibration stream (subset of The Pile/RedPajama/Wikipedia) to predict token difficulty labels defined by FP16 vs NF4 next-token NLL delta > k. Use logistic loss.
  - Freeze W,b. Then learn thresholds tau with STE on a 512-sample validation set to meet a global accuracy-loss budget (e.g., delta MMLU < 0.3) while minimizing E[s_t].
- Mixed-precision execution path
  - Activations and KV defaults: pack to 4-bit blocks. For tokens with s_t > 1, transiently up-cast to 8-bit by palette lookup through preloaded P8.
  - KV cache relayout: write each token’s K,V in 4b or 8b per s_t. Maintain a 2-bit header per 16-token block encoding stored precision. When reading, use precision = max(s_query, s_key). Implement read as a fused gather + unpack kernel (prototype in Triton; Python fallback can branch in PyTorch for correctness tests).
  - GEMM: prototype Triton matmul kernels that accept a per-row 1-bit mask selecting 4-bit/8-bit tiles with fixed tile ordering to avoid divergence. For first pass, emulate by two matmuls (4b and 8b) and concatenate outputs per mask; use the kernel to measure speed once correct.

Metrics
- Accuracy: lm-eval harness scores for MMLU avg, HellaSwag acc, GSM8K EM (8-shot), ARC-c/e acc
- Throughput: tokens/s for prefill and decode; latency P50/P99 (CUDA events)
- Memory: torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated and steady-state KV cache size
- Average precision budget E[s_t] and fraction of tokens at each score

Ablations
- No cache-relayout: store KV uniformly (4b or 8b); keep token-wise activation switching
- Random mask with matched E[s_t]
- Value-only palette switch (keys fixed to 4b)
- Predictor replaced by entropy threshold on logits

Procedure
- For each model and task:
  1) Run FP16 to collect reference metrics.
  2) Run each baseline.
  3) Run HAT-Q with calibrated thresholds. Log E[s_t], token histogram, accuracy, speed, memory.
  4) Run ablations.
- Repeat with 3 seeds for GSM8K few-shot sampling variation.

Expected outcomes
- MMLU drop <0.2 avg vs FP16; HellaSwag <0.1; GSM8K EM within 0.3%.
- Throughput +18% (7B) and +22% (13B) over static NF4; P99 latency ~15% better.
- KV memory reduced 28% vs uniform 8-bit and ~12% vs uniform 4-bit due to header compression.
- Ablations: random mask substantially worse; value-only switch drops long-range tasks more; removing cache-relayout erases KV memory wins and hurts long-context accuracy.

Implementation tips
- Use lm-eval-harness for consistency; cache prompts to avoid data loader variance.
- Warm up 200 tokens before timing; measure prefill and decode separately.
- Use torch.compile(dynamic=True) if available to cut Python overhead; Triton kernel behind a feature flag.


2) Experiment B: Long-context scaling and KV-cache effectiveness
Goal / hypothesis
- Demonstrate that HAT-Q’s cache-relayout and token-aware precision materially improve memory footprint and accuracy at 16k–32k contexts with minimal speed overhead.

Tasks
- Longeval (16k) and NarrativeQA-Long 32k subset; if unavailable, use LongBench or synthetic retrieval QA with 32k concatenations.

Setup
- Models: Llama-2-13B and Mistral-7B extended with RoPE scaling to 32k (e.g., llama.cpp rope-scaling or Position Interpolation via implementable config).
- Prompts: construct long contexts by concatenating documents with target spans near the end; ensure retrieval requires earlier segments.

Conditions
- FP16 (reference, may require tensor parallel or 2xA100)
- Static NF4 with uniform 8b KV; Static NF4 with uniform 4b KV
- HAT-Q full (predictor + cache-relayout)
- HAT-Q without cache-relayout (write/read KV at fixed precision = 4b or 8b)

Measurements
- Exact match / F1 on NarrativeQA-Long; LongBench/Longeval task metric
- Max reachable context length without OOM (increment 8k -> 32k)
- KV-cache memory versus context length (report bytes/token and total GB)
- Prefill throughput (tokens/s) at long prompts and decode tokens/s for 512 tokens continuation
- E[s_t] as a function of position (early vs late tokens) and under attention-intensive queries

Procedure
- Run each condition at context lengths 8k, 16k, 24k, 32k.
- At 32k, stress test with 3 concurrent streams (torch.cuda.Stream) to emulate batch concurrency.
- Log attention maps for selected layers to correlate s_t>1 spikes with attention spikes during query turns.

Expected outcomes
- HAT-Q attains +2–3% EM on 32k NarrativeQA vs static 4-bit; similar or better than 8-bit at notably lower memory.
- Sustained KV memory savings: ~28% vs uniform 8-bit and ~12% vs uniform 4-bit; enables 32k without OOM on single A100 for 13B.
- Prefill throughput at parity or modestly higher; decode throughput improved from reduced KV bandwidth.
- Removing cache-relayout negates gains and harms accuracy when s_query > s_key.

Implementation notes
- KV packing: represent 4-bit as uint8 with two nibbles per byte; 8-bit as int8; maintain a header tensor of shape [layers, heads, seq//16] with 2-bit entries packed into uint8. Provide pure PyTorch reference and Triton-optimized pack/unpack kernels.
- To quantify read policy max(s_query, s_key), compute s_query from current token and s_key from stored header; dispatch to correct dequant path without Python branching inside kernel (masking and fixed tile order in Triton).


3) Experiment C: Importance predictor validity, budgeted calibration, and robustness
Goal / hypothesis
- Show that the token-level predictor identifies “hard” tokens better than entropy or random; thresholds can be calibrated to meet a global accuracy-loss budget while minimizing 8-bit usage; robustness holds under noisy/adversarial prompts.

Datasets
- Calibration: 5–10M tokens from a mix of Wikipedia, WebText, math word problems (GSM8K stems), and long-context samples (concatenated books/QA)
- Evaluation: held-out subsets of MMLU, GSM8K (8-shot), ARC-c/e, plus a long-context subset (e.g., NarrativeQA-Long smaller split)

Signals and labels
- Token difficulty label y_t = 1 if NLL_FP16(t) - NLL_NF4(t) > delta (e.g., 0.15 nats) or if gradient norm of output layer wrt h_t is in top 20%.
- Optionally include an “attention stress” label if token receives high cross-layer attention mass at the time of query.

Training and calibration
- Train the linear probe (W,b) on hidden state h_t to predict y_t with logistic loss; stop early to avoid overfit; freeze W,b.
- Budgeted error fine-tuning of thresholds tau via STE:
  - Objective: L = task_loss(HAT-Q; tau) + lambda * max(0, E[s_t] - B), or constrained optimization with penalty ensuring delta accuracy <= target.
  - Use 512 calibration sequences; backpropagate through quantization gates with STE; update only tau.
  - Sweep B (precision budget) to generate a Pareto curve accuracy vs E[s_t].

Comparators
- Entropy threshold on softmax logits; margin threshold (top1-top2)
- Random masks matched to E[s_t]

Robustness conditions
- Prompt noise: randomly drop 10% of prompt tokens or replace with UNK; report delta accuracy
- Adversarial punctuation injection: insert bursts of punctuation and brackets every k tokens; report delta accuracy and E[s_t] changes

Metrics
- Predictor ROC-AUC and PR-AUC for y_t; calibration curve (pred score vs true difficulty rate)
- Accuracy vs budget curves for HAT-Q, entropy threshold, and random
- E[s_t] reduction at fixed accuracy threshold; fraction of tokens promoted to 8-bit in CoT reasoning turns
- Robustness: additional degradation vs FP16 under noise/adversary; change in E[s_t]

Procedure
- Collect FP16 and NF4 token-wise NLLs on calibration set to build labels.
- Train probe; freeze.
- Calibrate tau with STE for target budgets; evaluate on held-out tasks.
- Apply noise/adversarial transformations to prompts and re-evaluate.

Expected outcomes
- Probe AUC > 0.80; entropy threshold lower AUC; random at 0.5.
- For same accuracy loss (<0.3 MMLU, <0.3% GSM8K EM), HAT-Q uses fewer 8-bit tokens than entropy threshold by 15–25%.
- Robustness: additional degradation <0.5% vs FP16; E[s_t] automatically increases on perturbed prompts, indicating adaptive protection.

Implementation details (Python)
- Hidden-state tap: register forward hook on final block output to collect h_t per token during decoding.
- Tokenwise NLL: use teacher-forced forward to compute per-position cross-entropy.
- STE gates: implement with custom autograd Function that passes gradient 1 through thresholded comparisons.
- Budget sweeps and reliability diagrams via scikit-learn and matplotlib.


Common deliverables for all experiments
- Reproducible scripts:
  - quantize_palettes.py: build P4/P8 weight palettes and save
  - train_probe.py: fits W,b on calibration data
  - calibrate_thresholds.py: STE-based tau optimization under budget
  - run_eval.py: runs tasks with chosen config (FP16, baselines, HAT-Q variants)
  - long_context_eval.py: runs Experiment B at 8k–32k
  - microkernels.py: Triton pack/unpack and mixed-precision matmul
- Logs and plots:
  - Accuracy vs E[s_t] curves, throughput bars, memory vs context, predictor AUC, robustness deltas
- Config knobs: precision budget target, thresholds init, token group size for headers, palette group size, Triton tile size, seeds

Risk mitigations
- If Triton kernels are not ready, keep a correctness path using PyTorch ops; measure accuracy and E[s_t]; treat speed numbers as lower bound.
- If Bayesian Bits isn’t available, substitute with a simple layer-wise dynamic 4/8 switch baseline.
- If Longeval/NarrativeQA-Long data access is constrained, swap with LongBench tasks reaching 32k contexts.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Below is a consolidated, implementation-oriented experimental plan covering all items in Experiment Strategy. It integrates overlapping verification items where possible, maximizes reuse of existing Python libraries (Transformers, bitsandbytes, Triton, lm-eval-harness, scikit-learn), and assumes PyTorch as the primary framework. Where specialized kernels are not yet production-ready, correctness-first Python fallbacks are provided so accuracy, budget, and robustness findings remain reliable; speed metrics are clearly annotated as lower bounds in those cases.

EXPERIMENT A: End-to-end accuracy, throughput, and memory across diverse tasks

1) Goals and hypotheses
- Validate HAT-Q preserves accuracy while improving throughput/memory over standard 4/8-bit baselines.
- Confirm a learned token-importance predictor achieves lower average precision budget E[s_t] while retaining accuracy better than heuristics and random.

2) Models, HW, and software
- Models: Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, Mistral-7B (HuggingFace Transformers). Use permissive variants or local checkpoints as licensing allows.
- GPU: A100-80G; CUDA 12.2; PyTorch 2.4+; bitsandbytes 0.43+; Triton 2.2+; lm-eval-harness latest; Python 3.10/3.11.
- Recommended flags: torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True; cudnn.benchmark = True; ensure deterministic seed only for metric stability, not for perf microbench.

3) Tasks and data
- Knowledge & reasoning: MMLU (57 subs), HellaSwag, GSM8K (8-shot), ARC-c/e via lm-eval-harness.
- Sanity: Wikitext-2 perplexity for quick regressions.
- Prompt caching to avoid loader variance; fixed few-shot exemplars with 3 random seeds for GSM8K.

4) HAT-Q implementation (Python-feasible, correctness-first path plus optional Triton kernels)
4.1) Weight palettes (P4 NF4, P8 INT8)
- Load base model in FP16. Pre-quantize weights into two concurrent modules/palettes:
  - P4: bitsandbytes Linear4bit (NF4). This is the default path.
  - P8: bitsandbytes Linear8bitLt (INT8 per-channel symmetric). Keep per-channel scales.
- Keep both quantized representations resident in GPU memory. A simple wrapper selects per-token or per-row path. First-pass prototype does two matmuls (4-bit, 8-bit) for the rows corresponding to s_t and concatenates, to avoid writing custom CUDA immediately.

Example: quantize_palettes.py (skeleton)

import torch, os, json
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import bitsandbytes as bnb

# Save two copies: a NF4 model and an INT8 model checkpoints for palette access.
# The INT8 copy will be used in the 8-bit path; NF4 in the 4-bit path.

def load_palettes(model_name, device_map="auto"):
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, use_fast=True)
    # P4 NF4
    model_p4 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        torch_dtype=torch.float16,
        device_map=device_map,
        load_in_4bit=True,
        quantization_config=bnb.nn.quantization.QuantizationConfig(
            load_in_4bit=True,
            bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.float16,
            bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
            bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
        ),
    )
    # P8 INT8 (SmoothQuant/AWQ weight-only could also be swapped here if desired)
    model_p8 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_name,
        torch_dtype=torch.float16,
        device_map=device_map,
        load_in_8bit=True,
    )
    return tokenizer, model_p4, model_p8

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tok, p4, p8 = load_palettes("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf")
    # Optionally save references or state_dict handles as your infra requires

4.2) Importance predictor (linear probe + thresholds)
- Probe: s_hat = W h_t + b (scalar). Hidden state h_t is the model’s last-layer hidden at token t.
- Convert s_hat to s_t ∈ {0,1,2,3} via three thresholds tau = [t1, t2, t3]. Mapping: if s_hat <= t1 -> 0; (t1,t2] -> 1; (t2,t3] -> 2; > t3 -> 3.
- Precision mapping: s_t <= 1 uses 4-bit, s_t >= 2 uses 8-bit for activations/KV.
- Train W,b by logistic loss to predict token difficulty label y_t from calibration stream (5–10M tokens). Labels defined via FP16 vs NF4 NLL delta > k (e.g., 0.15 nats) OR gradient norm in top 20%.
- Freeze W,b. Then learn thresholds tau with STE on a 512-sequence calibration set to meet a global accuracy-loss budget while minimizing E[s_t]. Use next-token cross-entropy surrogate loss to make tau differentiable proxies feasible.

Probe training helper (train_probe.py; simplified)

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

class LinearProbe(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, 1)
    def forward(self, h):  # h: [B, T, H]
        return self.proj(h).squeeze(-1)

def logistic_loss(logits, labels):
    # logits: [N], labels in {0,1}
    return F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, labels.float())

# You will need a dataset that yields (hidden_states, labels). See Experiment C data collection.

def train_probe(model_fp16, model_nf4, dataloader, hidden_size, epochs=1, lr=1e-3, device="cuda"):
    probe = LinearProbe(hidden_size).to(device)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(probe.parameters(), lr=lr)
    model_fp16.eval(); model_nf4.eval()
    for e in range(epochs):
        for batch in dataloader:
            # batch should include precomputed hidden states h_t and labels y_t (see Experiment C)
            h_t, y_t = batch["h"].to(device), batch["y"].to(device)
            with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(enabled=False):
                logits = probe(h_t)  # [B, T]
                loss = logistic_loss(logits.reshape(-1), y_t.reshape(-1))
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return probe

Threshold calibration via STE (calibrate_thresholds.py; simplified)

class STEGate(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        return (x > 0).float()
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        return grad_output  # straight-through

class Thresholds(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, init_vals=( -0.5, 0.0, 0.5 )):
        super().__init__()
        self.tau = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(init_vals, dtype=torch.float32))
    def forward(self, s_hat):
        t1, t2, t3 = self.tau[0], self.tau[1], self.tau[2]
        g1 = STEGate.apply(s_hat - t1)
        g2 = STEGate.apply(s_hat - t2)
        g3 = STEGate.apply(s_hat - t3)
        # produce s_t in {0,1,2,3}
        s_t = g1 + g2 + g3  # since each gate adds 1 when passed
        return s_t.clamp(0,3)

# Calibrate tau to minimize CE + lambda * max(0, E[s_t] - B)

def calibrate_thresholds(model_hatq, probe, thresholds, calib_loader, B=1.2, lmbda=0.1, steps=200, lr=5e-3):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([thresholds.tau], lr=lr)
    for step, batch in zip(range(steps), calib_loader):
        # Run HAT-Q with probe+thresholds to produce s_t and perform forward on calib batch to compute CE.
        # Use next-token cross-entropy as surrogate objective; ensure the per-token precision follows s_t.
        ce_loss, E_s = model_hatq.forward_with_budget_loss(batch, probe, thresholds)
        penalty = torch.clamp(E_s - B, min=0.0)
        loss = ce_loss + lmbda * penalty
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return thresholds

4.3) Mixed-precision execution path and KV cache relayout
- At decode, tap the last hidden state h_t, compute s_hat via probe, derive s_t via thresholds. Map s_t to 4b/8b decisions for both activations and KV.
- KV cache write: write each token’s K,V in 4b or 8b block according to s_t, plus a 2-bit header per 16-token block encoding stored precision class. For now, use a PyTorch nibble-packing fallback for correctness.
- KV cache read for attention: use precision = max(s_query, s_key). In kernels, avoid branching by processing tiles in fixed order with masks. In Python fallback, we can branch while correctness-testing.
- GEMM path: initial prototype groups rows by mask (4b vs 8b), calls into respective bnb matmul, then concatenates outputs in correct order. Later, replace with a Triton kernel that accepts a per-row 1-bit mask.

Reference nibble packing utilities (microkernels.py; PyTorch + optional Triton)

import torch

def pack_nibbles(x_u8):
    # x_u8: uint8 values in [0,15], shape (..., 2K)
    x_even = x_u8[..., 0::2]
    x_odd  = x_u8[..., 1::2]
    packed = (x_odd << 4) | x_even
    return packed  # shape (..., K)

def unpack_nibbles(packed):
    even = packed & 0x0F
    odd  = (packed >> 4) & 0x0F
    out = torch.stack([even, odd], dim=-1).flatten(-2)
    return out

# 2-bit header packing for 16-token blocks; header entries in {0,1,2,3}

def pack_headers(s_tokens):
    # s_tokens: [T] s_t in 0..3; pack per 4 entries into a byte
    T = s_tokens.shape[0]
    pad = (4 - (T % 4)) % 4
    s_pad = torch.nn.functional.pad(s_tokens, (0, pad))
    s_pad = s_pad.reshape(-1,4)
    b0 = s_pad[:,0]
    b1 = s_pad[:,1] << 2
    b2 = s_pad[:,2] << 4
    b3 = s_pad[:,3] << 6
    return (b0 | b1 | b2 | b3).to(torch.uint8)

def unpack_headers(bytes_u8, T):
    bits = torch.stack([
        bytes_u8 & 0x03,
        (bytes_u8 >> 2) & 0x03,
        (bytes_u8 >> 4) & 0x03,
        (bytes_u8 >> 6) & 0x03,
    ], dim=-1).flatten()
    return bits[:T].to(torch.int32)

Integration wrapper for per-step decode (run_eval.py excerpt)

class HATQWrapper(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model_p4, model_p8, probe, thresholds, tokenizer):
        super().__init__()
        self.model_p4 = model_p4
        self.model_p8 = model_p8
        self.probe = probe.eval().requires_grad_(False)
        self.thresholds = thresholds
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        # KV cache storage handles; initialize on first use
        self.kv_store = None

    @torch.no_grad()
    def step(self, input_ids, past_key_values, attention_mask):
        # 1) Run the cheaper P4 path to get hidden states h_t for probe (or tap from model forward hooks)
        out = self.model_p4(
            input_ids=input_ids,
            past_key_values=past_key_values,
            attention_mask=attention_mask,
            output_hidden_states=True,
            use_cache=True,
        )
        h_last = out.hidden_states[-1][:, -1, :]  # [B, H], last token hidden for probe
        s_hat = self.probe(h_last.unsqueeze(1))  # [B, 1]
        s_t = self.thresholds(s_hat).squeeze(-1).long()  # 0..3
        eight_bit_mask = (s_t >= 2)
        # 2) Recompute the token with chosen precision. Prototype: group by mask.
        #    For correctness, we recompute one step with P8 if eight_bit_mask else P4.
        model = self.model_p8 if eight_bit_mask.any().item() else self.model_p4
        out2 = model(
            input_ids=input_ids,
            past_key_values=past_key_values,
            attention_mask=attention_mask,
            use_cache=True,
        )
        # 3) Logits for sampling/greedy; update KV cache externally if using custom storage
        return out2.logits[:, -1, :], out2.past_key_values, s_t

Note: The above is a simple, correctness-first path at token granularity that will under-report throughput gains; the Triton kernel path should replace recomputation by directly executing masked tiles.

4.4) Baselines
- FP16 reference: standard HF inference path.
- Static NF4 (weights) + uniform 8-bit activations or uniform 4/8 KV: load_in_4bit, optionally store KV as fp8_e4m3/e5m2 via torch.float8 if available, otherwise int8 nibble.
- SmoothQuant 8-bit: HuggingFace integration or llm.int8 path.
- AWQ 4-bit: load AWQ quantized weights via awq library if available; otherwise use public AWQ checkpoints.
- Naive ‘critical-token 8-bit’: compute logit entropy per step; s_t = 3 if entropy > threshold else 0. Threshold tuned on calibration set to match E[s_t] of HAT-Q.
- Bayesian Bits (if available). If not, substitute a simple layer-wise dynamic 4/8 switch baseline using activation norms.

4.5) Metrics and measurement
- Accuracy: lm-eval-harness tasks. Cache the tokenizer and adapters, pin seeds. For GSM8K 8-shot, evaluate with 3 seeds and report mean ± std.
- Throughput: tokens/s measured separately for prefill and decode; CUDA events with 200-token warmup; report P50 and P99 latency per token.
- Memory: torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats(); record max_memory_allocated; measure KV cache size directly by bytes per token and total bytes; compute E[s_t] and token-level histogram.

Timing utilities (snippet)

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        torch.cuda.synchronize(); self.start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        self.end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        self.start.record(); return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        self.end.record(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
        self.ms = self.start.elapsed_time(self.end)

# usage: with Timer() as t: ...; print(t.ms)

4.6) Procedure
- For each model:
  1) Prepare calibration data; collect labels; train probe; calibrate thresholds (see Experiment C for details).
  2) Evaluate FP16 reference across tasks; record metrics.
  3) Evaluate baselines: Static NF4 + uniform KV, SmoothQuant 8-bit, AWQ 4-bit, entropy heuristic, Bayesian Bits substitute.
  4) Evaluate HAT-Q with calibrated thresholds; record E[s_t], token histogram, accuracy, throughput, memory.
  5) Ablations: no cache-relayout (uniform KV), random mask with matched E[s_t], value-only palette switch, entropy-based predictor.
  6) GSM8K: repeat with 3 seeds.
- Ensure 200-token warmup before timing; run each timing scenario 3 times and report median.

4.7) Expected outcomes (to be verified)
- MMLU drop < 0.2 avg vs FP16; HellaSwag < 0.1; GSM8K EM within 0.3%.
- Throughput +18% (7B) and +22% (13B) vs static NF4; P99 latency ~15% better.
- KV memory reduced ~28% vs uniform 8-bit, ~12% vs uniform 4-bit.
- Ablations: random mask degrades accuracy; value-only hurts long-context tasks; removing cache-relayout erodes memory and long-context accuracy.

EXPERIMENT B: Long-context scaling and KV-cache effectiveness

1) Goals and hypotheses
- Show that cache-relayout and token-aware precision improve memory footprint and accuracy at 16k–32k contexts, with minimal speed overhead.

2) Setup and data
- Models: Llama-2-13B and Mistral-7B with RoPE scaling to 32k. In Transformers, set model.config.rope_scaling = {"type": "linear", "factor": 4} (or NTK-aware scaling if available), then model.set_default_generate_kwargs(max_length=32768) if needed.
- Datasets: Longeval (16k), NarrativeQA-Long 32k subset; fallback: LongBench or synthetic retrieval QA with concatenated documents.
- Prompts: Concatenate multi-document contexts; answers dependent on earlier spans; ensure retrieval nature to exercise attention.

3) Conditions
- FP16 reference (tensor parallel or 2x A100 if needed).
- Static NF4 + uniform 8b KV; Static NF4 + uniform 4b KV.
- HAT-Q full (predictor + cache-relayout).
- HAT-Q without cache-relayout (fixed KV precision = 4b or 8b; still token-wise activations).

4) Measurements
- Task metrics: NarrativeQA EM/F1; Longeval/LongBench task metrics.
- Max reachable context length without OOM (increase 8k -> 32k stepwise).
- KV memory per token and total GB, measured at steady state; report bytes/token vs context length.
- Prefill throughput and decode throughput (512-token continuation); P50/P99 latency.
- E[s_t] vs position index; diagnostics for attention spikes at query turns.

5) Implementation notes
- KV formats:
  - 4-bit KV: quantize and pack as uint8 nibbles [0..15], per head. Store per-head scales/zero-points per 16 or 32 elements for dequant.
  - 8-bit KV: int8 + per-channel scale; pack separately.
  - Header: 2 bits per token, packed per 4 tokens into 1 byte, or per 16 tokens if grouping; we recommend per 16 tokens with a small LUT.

6) Procedure
- For each model and each context length (8k, 16k, 24k, 32k):
  - Run each condition; record metrics.
  - For 32k, stress with 3 CUDA streams (concurrent batch=3) during decode; measure throughput and latency.

- Stop when OOM occurs; note maximum attainable length for each condition.

7) Expected outcomes
- HAT-Q improves EM by 2–3% on 32k NarrativeQA vs static 4-bit; parity or better than 8-bit at lower memory.
- KV memory savings ~28% vs uniform 8-bit and ~12% vs uniform 4-bit; enables 32k on single A100 for 13B.
- Prefill throughput near parity; decode throughput improved thanks to reduced KV bandwidth.
- Removing cache-relayout negates memory and harms accuracy when s_query > s_key.

EXPERIMENT C: Importance predictor validity, budgeted calibration, and robustness

1) Goals and hypotheses
- Validate that the probe identifies “hard” tokens better than entropy or random.
- Show thresholds can be tuned to meet accuracy-loss budget while minimizing 8-bit usage.
- Demonstrate robustness under prompt noise and adversarial punctuation.

2) Calibration and evaluation data
- Calibration: 5–10M tokens sampled from Wikipedia, WebText, GSM8K stems, and long-context concatenations.
- Evaluation: held-out subsets of MMLU, GSM8K (8-shot), ARC-c/e, and NarrativeQA-Long small split.

3) Signals, labels, and data collection pipeline
- Compute teacher-forced per-token NLL under FP16 and NF4 on calibration corpus.
- Difficulty label y_t = 1 if NLL_FP16(t) - NLL_NF4(t) > delta (e.g., 0.15 nats), OR if gradient norm of LM head wrt h_t in top 20% (optional multi-signal OR).
- Optionally, compute attention stress if a token attracts high attention mass across layers at query time.

Data collection code (collect_labels.py excerpt)

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def per_token_nll(model, input_ids, attention_mask):
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, labels=input_ids)
        # out.loss is average; we need per-token
        logits = out.logits[:, :-1, :]
        targets = input_ids[:, 1:]
        ce = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.reshape(-1), reduction="none")
        return ce.view(targets.shape)  # [B, T-1]

# Given model_fp16 and model_nf4, compute delta NLL and labels

def build_labels(model_fp16, model_nf4, dataloader, delta=0.15):
    labels, h_states = [], []
    for batch in dataloader:
        ids = batch["input_ids"].to("cuda")
        attn = batch["attention_mask"].to("cuda")
        ce_fp16 = per_token_nll(model_fp16, ids, attn)
        ce_nf4  = per_token_nll(model_nf4,  ids, attn)
        y = (ce_nf4 - ce_fp16 > delta).to(torch.int8)
        # Collect hidden states from fp16 run for probe training
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = model_fp16(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=attn, output_hidden_states=True)
            h_last = out.hidden_states[-1][:, :-1, :]  # align with ce shape
        labels.append(y.cpu()); h_states.append(h_last.cpu())
    return torch.cat(h_states, dim=0), torch.cat(labels, dim=0)

4) Probe training and threshold calibration
- Train probe (LinearProbe) with logistic loss; early stop via held-out split.
- Calibrate thresholds tau with STE on 512 sequences; objective: surrogate CE + lambda * max(0, E[s_t] - B); sweep budget B to get accuracy vs E[s_t] Pareto.

5) Comparators
- Entropy threshold: compute entropy H(p) at each step; select 8-bit if H > tau_ent tuned to match E[s_t]. Margin threshold (top1 - top2) is an alternative.
- Random mask: sample Bernoulli to match E[s_t].

6) Robustness tests
- Prompt noise: drop 10% of prompt tokens uniformly at random or replace with [UNK]; ensure alignment of labels/answers.
- Adversarial punctuation injection: insert sequences of punctuation/brackets every k tokens.
- Report delta accuracy vs clean prompts, and how E[s_t] adapts.

Robustness transforms (robustness.py excerpt)

import torch

def drop_tokens(input_ids, drop_prob=0.1, pad_token_id=0):
    mask = torch.rand_like(input_ids.float()) > drop_prob
    out = input_ids.clone()
    out[~mask] = pad_token_id
    return out

def inject_punctuation(input_ids, punct_token_id, every_k=20, repeat=3):
    B, T = input_ids.shape
    out = []
    for b in range(B):
        seq = input_ids[b].tolist()
        aug = []
        for i, tok in enumerate(seq):
            aug.append(tok)
            if i % every_k == 0 and i>0:
                aug.extend([punct_token_id]*repeat)
        out.append(torch.tensor(aug[:T], dtype=torch.long))
    return torch.stack(out, dim=0)

7) Metrics and diagnostics
- Predictor ROC-AUC, PR-AUC for y_t; reliability diagram (score vs difficulty rate).
- Accuracy vs budget curves for HAT-Q vs entropy vs random.
- E[s_t] reduction at fixed accuracy; fraction of tokens escalated in CoT segments.
- Robustness: additional degradation vs FP16; observe E[s_t] increase under noise/adversary.

8) Expected outcomes
- Probe AUC > 0.80; entropy heuristic lower AUC; random ~0.5.
- For same accuracy loss (<0.3 MMLU; <0.3% GSM8K EM), HAT-Q uses 15–25% fewer 8-bit tokens than entropy.
- Robustness: <0.5% extra degradation vs FP16; E[s_t] increases adaptively on perturbed prompts.

INTEGRATED EVALUATION PIPELINE

1) lm-eval-harness integration
- Use lm_eval.api to evaluate models that expose generate and loglikelihood APIs.
- Wrap HAT-Q into a model class that conforms to lm-eval; for baselines, reuse built-ins. Cache prompts and set seeds.

Example CLI (conceptual)

python run_eval.py \
  --model_name meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf \
  --method hatq \
  --probe_ckpt probe.pt --tau_ckpt tau.pt \
  --tasks mmlu,hellaswag,arc_easy,arc_challenge,gsm8k \
  --shots 0 --gsm8k_shots 8 --seeds 3 \
  --measure_throughput --measure_memory

2) Throughput and memory measurement methodology
- Warmup: 200 tokens prefill and 200 decode tokens; discard.
- Prefill timing: feed the full prompt; record tokens/s.
- Decode timing: generate 512 tokens auto-regressively.
- Latency: record per-token P50 and P99 with CUDA events.
- Memory: report torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated/reset; compute KV bytes/token based on actual packed buffers; provide both peak and steady-state.

ABLATIONS (applies across Experiments A and B)
- No cache-relayout: store KV uniformly (choose 4b or 8b), still do token-wise activation precision.
- Random mask, matched E[s_t].
- Value-only palette switch: keys forced to 4b.
- Predictor replaced by entropy threshold; thresholds tuned to match E[s_t].

MICROKERNELS AND PERFORMANCE PATH (prototype)

- Mixed-precision matmul skeleton in Triton that takes a per-row mask:
  - Inputs: A (activations, possibly upcasted using P8), W4 (NF4) and W8 (INT8) palettes, mask m ∈ {0,1}^{M} for rows.
  - Strategy: process tiles in fixed order; for each row tile, select W4 or W8 path via masking to avoid divergence in inner loops; accumulate partial results into O.
  - Fallback: split rows by mask, call bnb 4-bit and 8-bit GEMMs separately, then scatter back.

RISK MITIGATION AND RELIABILITY
- If Triton kernels are not ready, keep Python/bnb correctness path and treat throughput as a lower bound. Accuracy, E[s_t], and memory measurements remain valid.
- Use 3-run medians for timing. Include NVML-based cross-check of memory if desired (pynvml) to corroborate torch-reported stats.
- Control seeds for evaluation while leaving cuBLAS autotuning enabled for fair perf.
- Validate each component independently: probe AUC, correct pack/unpack round-trips, KV read policy max(s_query, s_key) via unit tests.

COMMON DELIVERABLES

1) Reproducible scripts (CLI args with Hydra/argparse)
- quantize_palettes.py: builds P4/P8 palettes via bitsandbytes and saves references.
- collect_labels.py: computes per-token NLLs (FP16 vs NF4), builds difficulty labels, and caches hidden states.
- train_probe.py: fits W,b on calibration data; saves probe.pt.
- calibrate_thresholds.py: STE-based tau optimization using a 512-sequence set; saves tau.pt.
- run_eval.py: runs Experiment A with FP16, baselines, HAT-Q variants; logs accuracy, throughput, memory, E[s_t].
- long_context_eval.py: runs Experiment B at 8k–32k, reports OOM points, EM/F1, KV bytes/token, throughput; supports concurrent streams.
- microkernels.py: pack/unpack nibble utils and Triton kernels behind a feature flag; Python fallbacks.

2) Logs and plots
- Accuracy vs E[s_t] curves; throughput bars by model and condition; memory vs context length; predictor ROC/PR; robustness deltas; E[s_t] vs position.
- Store JSON and CSV logs; produce Matplotlib/Seaborn figures.

3) Config knobs
- Precision budget target B, thresholds init values, token group size for headers, palette group size, Triton tile size, seeds, entropy thresholds for baselines, rope scaling factor/type.

4) Unit tests and sanity checks
- Verify pack_nibbles(unpack_nibbles(x)) = x for random tensors.
- Verify header packing round-trip; verify max(s_query, s_key) policy matches intended path by synthetic masks.
- Compare logits under FP16 vs HAT-Q at small contexts to ensure bounded drift pre-calibration.

SUMMARY OF HOW ITEMS ARE INTEGRATED WITHOUT EXCESSIVE OVERLAP
- Experiment A establishes end-to-end correctness, accuracy, throughput, and memory across diverse tasks; ablations included.
- Experiment B specifically targets long-context scaling where KV-cache policies matter most; reports memory/accuracy trade-offs beyond what A covers.
- Experiment C isolates the predictor and calibration mechanism with diagnostic metrics (AUC, Pareto curves) and robustness; it supplies the probe and tau artifacts needed by A and B.
- Shared infrastructure (palettes, predictor, cache relayout, timing/memory tools) is reused across A, B, and C to reduce redundancy and improve reliability.

EXPECTED FINDINGS RECAP (to be validated)
- Accuracy: HAT-Q closely tracks FP16 on reasoning tasks and surpasses static 4-bit on long-context QA.
- Performance: +18–22% throughput over static NF4 and improved P99 latency via reduced KV bandwidth.
- Memory: ~28% KV savings vs uniform 8-bit and ~12% vs uniform 4-bit thanks to header compression and selective 8-bit use.
- Predictor: explains >80% of accuracy retention; random masks fail; HAT-Q more budget-efficient than entropy heuristic.
- Robustness: <0.5% additional degradation vs FP16; E[s_t] increases adaptively under noise/adversary.
